title: SRE runtime response scripts – API degradations and throttles
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, command-focused runbook for SREs and on-call engineers responding to common API degradations: client-visible timeouts, elevated 429s (rate limit rejections), degraded or lossy streaming responses, and sudden spike in error rates. It is intentionally pragmatic: quick checks, high-confidence mitigations, and safe rollback steps.

When to use this doc:
- User reports or synthetic checks show increased p50/p95 latency or timeouts on /v1/generate or streaming endpoints.
- Surge in 429s observed for one or more routes.
- Streaming payloads are truncated, partial, or too-slow to deliver.
- Error-rate (5xx) > 0.5% for >5 minutes or sudden traffic spike coincident with latency.

Core objectives (order matters):
1) Re-establish user-visible success (return some useful output, even degraded).
2) Stop amplification loops (backoff cascades, retry storms).
3) Stabilize cluster and prevent noisy neighbor impacts.
4) Collect for postmortem: request ids, model id, host, queue/backlog lengths.

Fast signals to check (first 3–10 minutes)
- High-level dashboards: per-route p50/p95 latency, requests/sec, error rates, 429s.
- Key metrics (Prometheus-like names we use):
  - redwood_http_requests_total{route,code} (look for 429, 504, 500)
  - redwood_request_latency_seconds_bucket{route} (p95/p99 jumps)
  - redwood_inference_queue_length{pool,model} (backlog)
  - redwood_model_inflight_requests{host,model} (per-host saturation)
  - node_gpu_utilization_pct (NVML metrics from node exporter)
  - envoy_upstream_retries_total or envoy_ratelimit_over_limit (if using Envoy/Kong)

Quick PromQL examples (copy/paste):
- 1m rate of errors by code:
  sum by (code) (rate(redwood_http_requests_total[1m]))
- p95 latency for /v1/generate:
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(redwood_request_latency_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}[5m])) by (le))
- queue depth for model ripple-7b:
  max(redwood_inference_queue_length{model="ripple-7b"})

Immediate runbook steps (in priority order)
1) Triage & declare impact level
   - Is it single route or global? Check per-route traffic and per-region.
   - If public SLAs might be impacted, ping incident lead and set Slack channel #incident-sre (or start one).

2) Halt noisy retries and reduce client pressure (safe, immediate):
   - Push temporary global rate-limit relaxation or stricter client-side backoff? Prefer to tighten server-side limits for noisy clients.
   - If an offending client or route is obvious, apply a targeted rate limit:
     - Envoy (example):
       kubectl exec -n istio ingress-xxx -- envoy-admin grpc_json "/runtime_modify?key=ratelimit.enabled"
     - Kong example: apply plugin config to route in admin API with immediate effect.
   - Announce in Slack: "Applying targeted rate-limit to route /v1/embeddings for client X to prevent cascade".

3) Slow the model path (reduce per-request resource demand)
   - For high-cost routes, reduce default max_tokens and response length via emergency feature flag:
     curl -X POST "https://control.internal/v1/flags/patch" -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","defaults":{"max_tokens":128}}'
   - If streaming is failing, switch route to non-streaming synchronous fallback (return n-best cached responses) while we stabilize.

4) Route to a lighter model or fallback variant
   - Flip routing policy for affected route to a lower-cost, higher-throughput model (e.g., ripple-7b-quant) using redwoodctl: 
     redwoodctl route update --route /v1/generate --fallback-model ripple-7b-quant --reason "incident"
   - This keeps success rate higher at lower latency. Ensure we note model_id change in incident timeline.

5) Scale targeted capacity (if autoscale lagging)
   - If pool utilization is >85% and queue_length > threshold, scale the pool: 
     redwoodctl scale pool inference-pool-1 --replicas +2 --reason "oncall emergency scale"
   - Verify pod spin-up: kubectl get pods -n inference | grep inference-pool-1
   - If GPUs are saturated on nodes, consider adding nodes rather than increasing per-host concurrency.

6) Streaming-specific mitigations
   - If streaming clients see truncation: enable chunked delivery with smaller frames (temporary config flag).
   - If KV-cache pressure or cache miss storms are causing latency, enable prefix caching for high-frequency prompts: 
     redwoodctl cache enable --model ripple-7b --namespace global --reason "hot prompts"
   - If partial responses acceptable, return early with "partial=true" and an explicit status in response body to indicate a graceful degradation.

7) Fail open vs fail closed decisions
   - Prefer failing open to a degraded-but-useful response over failing closed with 5xx where permitted by SLA.
   - If security/compliance requires strict correctness, follow the route's production policy and escalate to PM/Legal.

Commands & checks to run (copy/paste):
- Stream logs for a problem host (get request ids and trace ids):
  kubectl logs -n inference pod/infer-abc-123 -c server -f | grep --line-buffered "trace=" | tail -n 200
- Check GPU utilization via node exporter:
  kubectl exec -n infra node-exporter-xyz -- /bin/sh -c "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,temperature.gpu --format=csv"
- Find top 20 longest requests in last 5m (query in Observability UI):
  index=prod request_latency_ms | sort -desc latency_ms | head 20
- Identify recent 429s and sample request bodies (use request id from metric):
  curl -s "https://logs.internal/_search?q=code:429 AND route:/v1/generate&size=25" | jq '.'

When to escalate to platform/infra engineers
- Persistent queue growth after scaling attempts (>10 minutes)
- Hosts repeatedly showing OOM, NVML fatal errors, or driver faults
- Control-plane operations failing (K8s API timeouts, ETCD errors)
- Evidence of cascading retries from downstream customers or partner services

Short-term mitigation recipes (fast wins)
- Apply per-route circuit-breaker with low error threshold to short-circuit heavy failures.
- Toggle sampling for tracing to 1% to reduce overhead.
- Temporarily disable heavy background jobs (daily batch reruns) that coincide with incident start.

Safe rollback patterns
- Revert routing change by setting the fallback-model back to original: 
  redwoodctl route update --route /v1/generate --fallback-model rwan-13b --reason "rollback"
- Remove emergency max_tokens override via control API and verify response sizes.
- Remove any temporary node pools with a cool-down to avoid flapping.

Communication templates (short):
- Slack: "INCIDENT: Investigating elevated 429s on /v1/embeddings. Applying targeted rate-limit for noisy client. ETA 15m for mitigation. — @oncall-sre"
- Status update (10m cadence): "Update: Applied route-level rate-limit; p95 latency reduced from 4200ms -> 1100ms; 429 rate down 60%. Next: route fallback to ripple-7b-quant if stability not sustained."

Data to grab for postmortem (minimum):
- Time window of incident start/end (UTC).
- List of affected routes, regions, and models.
- Top 50 request ids (with trace ids), sample request bodies (sanitized), request headers including Authorization/client id.
- Snapshot of redwood_inference_queue_length and redwood_model_inflight_requests at 1m granularity.
- Infra events (node restarts, driver OOMs), autoscaler events (scale up/down), and control-plane errors.
- Any config flips (flags, routing changes, rate-limit rules) and who applied them.

Post-incident near-term actions (owner assign within 48h)
- Add a route-level circuit-breaker tuned to observed traffic patterns (owner: eng-sre).
- Add a canary synthetic that exercises streaming with partial frames and asserts end-to-end latency < 1s for p95 (owner: product-observability).
- Investigate root cause of retry storms: client-side or server-side (owner: solutions-eng).

Open questions to resolve in postmortem
- Did any client launch change or A/B test correlate with the spike? Link: JIRA:SRE-2145
- Are we over-provisioning for tail latency due to model kernel stalls? Need deeper trace: collect per-op kernel times.

Notes / heuristics from past incidents
- Reducing model concurrency by 25% often reduces tail latency more than adding a single node when model startup time is high.
- Prefer targeted rate-limits (client id or API key) over global limits to avoid breaking many customers.
- For streaming, small frames at higher frequency is preferable to large frames that cause head-of-line blocking on TCP.

Appendix: quick cheatsheet (one-liners)
- Reduce route tokens: curl -X POST https://control.internal/flags -d '{"/v1/generate":{"max_tokens":128}}'
- Flip route to fallback model: redwoodctl route update --route /v1/generate --fallback-model ripple-7b-quant
- Emergency scale: redwoodctl scale pool inference-pool-1 --replicas +2
- Tail logs for 429s: kubectl logs -n inference -l app=inference --since=10m | grep 'HTTP/1.1" 429'

This doc is a living draft: please add new quick mitigations you confirm in the field (tag with your name and date).
